Chapter 3: Navigating Bureaucracy and Sanctions—The Art of Survival
Imagine trying to run a business where every single decision—no matter how small—has to pass through a maze of approvals. That’s daily life in North Korea. The bureaucracy there is both a shield and a challenge. Picture filling out the same form three times, getting each copy officially stamped, and watching it disappear into an office lined with dusty old ledgers. If you’re a foreign business, you quickly learn that nothing moves fast. Progress demands patience and a whole lot of careful planning. But that’s just one part of the puzzle. Sanctions add a whole new level of difficulty. International rules dictate what you can import, export, and sometimes even talk about. Banking? That’s a constant headache. Sending money in or out of the country can take weeks, with payments vanishing into thin air and reappearing without explanation. And just when you think a deal is done, it might fall apart because a partner abroad suddenly gets nervous. The rules themselves? They’re always shifting. One day, a product’s cleared for sale. The next? It’s suddenly banned, no warning at all. Maybe your shipment arrives at the border, only to be held up by customs officials demanding new paperwork you didn’t even know existed. It’s in these moments that patience gets tested, and creativity becomes an absolute necessity. Local managers, who’ve been through this again and again, will tell you—never assume anything’s final. Always have a Plan B. When a crucial delivery gets delayed, the team doesn’t panic. Instead, they start juggling—maybe borrowing supplies from another factory, or shaking up the production schedule to keep things moving. Over time, you learn to expect the unexpected, and somehow, you figure out how to keep going. Here’s something that might surprise you: in North Korea, relationships matter far more than rules. Sometimes, a well-timed phone call, a shared meal, or even a simple gesture of respect can open doors paperwork never could. I’ll give you an example. After a long day of negotiations, a government official invites the foreign team out to a karaoke bar. For a few hours, the atmosphere relaxes, and barriers come down. The next morning, that project you’ve been waiting on suddenly gets the green light. It’s a powerful reminder—personal connections are often the real key to making things happen. Still, the risks are real. Every choice carries the potential for misunderstanding, and the consequences can be serious. That’s why foreign managers learn to tread carefully, double-check every detail, and keep meticulous records. Mistakes are costly, and if trust is broken, it’s tough to win it back. Yet, despite all these obstacles, there are moments that make it worthwhile. Maybe a new product line finally launches, bringing in much-needed revenue and creating jobs. Or a training program helps workers pick up new skills—lifting morale and productivity. Sure, these victories are hard-won, but they prove that, even in the toughest environments, real progress is possible. Living and working under sanctions teaches you to adapt. Plans change, setbacks become routine, and victories often come in small, hard-earned steps. But for those willing to stick with it, the rewards go beyond business. You get to witness firsthand the resilience and ingenuity of people who are determined to survive—and even thrive—no matter what obstacles they face.
